questions: Did these involuntary movements begin suddenly?
Do you feel that the affected hand sometimes moves on its own, without you intending it to?
Do you have weakness or loss of coordination in that hand?
Have you had a recent stroke, head injury, or brain surgery?
Do you have stiffness or slowness of movement on the same side?
Does the movement lessen when you are distracted or when you voluntarily use the hand?
Do you experience an uncomfortable urge or sensation before the hand moves?
Does performing the movement relieve that sensation?
Can you briefly stop the movement if you concentrate on doing so?
Do the movements disappear during sleep?
Are the movements worse when you are anxious, stressed, or being watched?
Does the hand ever interfere with or oppose what your other hand is trying to do?
Do you have numbness or an altered sense of ownership of that hand?
Are you taking levodopa, antipsychotic medication, anti-nausea medication, or stimulant medication?
Do similar involuntary movements affect your face, mouth, tongue, or the other arm or leg?
Do you have difficulty speaking, swallowing, or controlling your facial expressions?
Have these movements gradually worsened over weeks or months?
Have you noticed loss of dexterity, such as difficulty buttoning clothes or using utensils with that hand?
Does the affected hand assume abnormal fixed postures or become more abnormal when you try to use it?
Do you have balance problems or frequent falls?
Have you had changes in memory, judgment, or personality?
Has anyone in your biological family had similar movements or been diagnosed with Huntington disease?
Did the involuntary movements begin before the changes in memory, judgment, or personality?
Have you had episodes of loss of awareness, staring, or unusual smells or sensations suggestive of seizures?
Do the movements consist of brief, irregular, unpredictable jerks that flow from one body part to another?
Do you have involuntary movements of the tongue or repeated biting of the inside of your cheeks?
Have you developed difficulty walking, muscle stiffness, or unusually slow movements?
Have you had new psychiatric symptoms such as depression, irritability, hallucinations, or compulsive behavior?
Did the cognitive or behavioral changes begin suddenly over days to weeks?
Have you had a recent infection, cancer, or exposure to a new medication before these symptoms began?
Do you have vivid dream enactment, loss of smell, constipation, or marked fluctuations in alertness?
Do you have severe daytime sleepiness, disrupted sleep, or episodes of inability to move when falling asleep or waking?
Have you developed prominent autonomic symptoms such as unexplained blood-pressure changes, urinary retention, or abnormal sweating?
Is the affected hand clumsy for learned tasks, despite normal strength and sensation?
Does the hand perform apparently purposeful actions that you do not intend, such as grasping, groping, or touching objects?
Do you have difficulty recognizing objects by touch or identifying your own fingers?
Have you developed rapidly progressive memory loss or loss of independence over less than one year?
Has anyone observed repetitive stereotyped movements or compulsive behaviors involving the hand?
Have you had a persistently elevated or irritable mood with decreased need for sleep, increased energy, racing thoughts, or unusually increased goal-directed activity?
Are the hand movements repetitive, patterned, and similar each time rather than random or dance-like?
Do you repeat words, phrases, gestures, or other behaviors even when you do not intend to?
Have you developed loss of empathy, socially inappropriate behavior, dietary changes, or compulsive/ritualistic behavior?
Have you had a noticeable decline in language comprehension or word meaning despite normal speech mechanics?
Has a clinician observed emotional blunting or loss of insight into your behavioral changes?
orders: MRI brain with attention to the caudate nuclei and putamina
Peripheral-blood HTT CAG-repeat expansion genetic test
Serum TSH, free T4, vitamin B12, copper, ceruloplasmin, ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies, and anti–NMDA-receptor antibodies
Urine drug screen including stimulants and dopamine-blocking substances

Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted, FLAIR, susceptibility-weighted, and T1 volumetric sequences, specifically assessing the frontal and parietal cortices, corpus callosum, basal ganglia, and medial temporal lobes
Comprehensive neuropsychological assessment including executive function, inhibition, social cognition, memory, and language
Video-EEG monitoring with attempted capture of the abnormal movements
Bedside examination for functional movement disorder, including distractibility, entrainment, variability, suggestibility, and a Bereitschaftspotential assessment during movement initiation
Cerebrospinal-fluid examination including cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, 14-3-3 protein, and real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) prion assay
Serum and CSF neuronal surface/synaptic antibody testing including LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, DPPX, GAD65, and IgLON5 antibodies
Genetic testing for Huntington-disease phenocopies, including C9orf72, TBP/SCA17, JPH3, VPS13A, and PRNP expansions or pathogenic variants
FDG-PET brain scan to assess for frontotemporal, striatal, or other neurodegenerative hypometabolism
Formal movement-disorders examination with video documentation, specifically testing for chorea, dystonia, stereotypy, motor impersistence, distractibility, entrainment, and stimulus sensitivity
MRI brain review by a movement-disorders neuroradiologist, specifically assessing for caudate/putaminal atrophy, cortical atrophy, and structural lesions
Serum antiphospholipid and autoimmune vasculopathy evaluation repeated with ESR, CRP, ANA, ENA, and complement levels
Medication and supplement reconciliation with pharmacy records, specifically looking for prior dopamine-receptor–blocking or anticholinergic exposure
served: CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
chorea gene panel (VPS13A, JPH3, C9orf72, FRRS1L)
distribution of the movements (one side, both, face, limbs)
effect of voluntary action and anxiety
